findings.title: User-storage recovery codes are reusable and not sequential
findings.body: BackwardsCompatibilityUserStorage.isValid accepts a recovery code if any stored code equals the submitted value, and it never removes the matched code. After CredentialHelper.createRecoveryCodesCredential stores the codes in user storage, login calls credentialManager().isValid, which hits this method instead of RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialProvider (the component that consumes a locally stored code). Nothing in the authenticator updates the stored list afterward. A previously used code therefore keeps working forever, and any of the twelve codes is accepted regardless of the index RecoveryAuthnCodeInputLoginBean displays. Shoulder-surfing or replay of one code is enough to authenticate again. The new login test only submits the first code once, so it does not catch this.

findings.title: Recovery codes stored in plaintext
findings.body: updateCredential saves input.getChallengeResponse() straight into CredentialModel.credentialData. That value is the JSON array of raw recovery codes written by CredentialHelper.createRecoveryCodesCredential, and isValid later compares those strings with String.equals. The password branch in the same method hashes the secret with PasswordHashProvider before storing it. Recovery codes are password-equivalent; anyone who can read this provider's user map, or a storage implementation that persists the challenge response the same way, can log in as the user. Hash the codes (RecoveryAuthnCodesUtils.hashRawCode, or the RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel secret format) before persisting them, and compare hashes on validation.

findings.title: getCredentials drops id and resets usage
findings.body: getCredentials does not return the stored recovery-code CredentialModel. On every read it deserializes the original plaintext list and passes it to RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel.createFromValues, which builds a new all-unused model and does not keep the id assigned in updateCredential (recoveryCodesModel.setId). The id Keycloak sees is therefore null, so account-console deletion and removeStoredCredentialById cannot target the stored credential. The next-code number shown by RecoveryAuthnCodeInputLoginBean is always the first code, even after a code has been used, and any usage state a correct isValid would persist is discarded on the next read. Login keeps prompting for code 0.

findings.title: Recovery codes cannot be disabled
findings.body: disableCredentialType only clears OTP. For recovery-authn-codes it logs that the type is unsupported and leaves MyUser.recoveryCodes set. getDisableableCredentialTypesStream likewise only reports OTP, so the admin API and account console will not treat recovery codes as disableable. OTP removal in this class works because both methods handle OTP; recovery codes need the same treatment. After setup, a user cannot turn recovery codes off, isConfiguredFor stays true, and a browser flow that requires them keeps challenging for a code that cannot be removed.

findings.title: Exhausted user-storage recovery codes are not deleted
findings.body: After a successful recovery-code login the authenticator now loads the credential with RecoveryAuthnCodesUtils.getCredential, which prefers user storage, and if allCodesUsed() is true it calls removeStoredCredentialById and ignores the result. That API deletes a row in Keycloak's local credential store. A credential created when user storage's updateCredential returns true is not in that store. The model getCredentials returns also has a null id, because createFromValues does not preserve the id stored on the provider, so the remove call cannot match the federated credential either. The exhausted credential stays configured. The next login still runs this authenticator, and RecoveryAuthnCodeInputLoginBean then calls getNextRecoveryAuthnCode().get() with no remaining code, which throws and fails login with a server error instead of the reconfigure required action. Cleanup needs disableCredentialType (and the storage provider must honor it); removeStoredCredentialById alone does not clear user storage.

findings.title: Old local recovery codes survive user-storage create
findings.body: When user.credentialManager().updateCredential returns true, createRecoveryCodesCredential logs success and does not delete recovery-authn-codes credentials already stored in Keycloak's local store. Before this change, federated users always received local recovery codes, because user storage did not accept the type. After this change, a provider that returns true (including BackwardsCompatibilityUserStorage, which newly supports the type) stores the new set externally and leaves the previous local set in place. credentialManager().isValid still tries local credential providers when the user-storage check does not accept the submitted code, so the old codes remain valid after the user generates a new set. Regeneration does not revoke previously issued recovery codes. On a successful user-storage write, existing local credentials of this type must be removed.

findings.title: Recovery-code storage test misses reuse and removal
findings.body: testRecoveryKeysSetupAndLogin writes recovery codes, asserts they are absent from Keycloak's DB and present in the user-storage map, and logs in once with code index 0. It never reuses that code, never checks that the next login asks for the next index, never submits an out-of-order code, never regenerates codes after a local credential already exists, and never disables or deletes the credential. Those are the paths this PR gets wrong: isValid accepts any code and does not consume it, getCredentials rebuilds an unused set with a null id, disableCredentialType ignores the type, and a later user-storage create does not revoke an older local set. The test passes while recovery codes remain reusable and irremovable.
